text: The London Marathon has three colour-coded starts in Greenwich Park — Blue (elite men + championship), Red (elite women + most Good-for-Age), and Green (remaining runners). All three merge near Woolwich Road by mile 3. Know your start colour and follow signs from your designated assembly area.
label: Start Logistics

text: Baggage buses are located near each start area in Greenwich Park. You must use the official clear bag provided and label it with your runner number. Bags are transported to The Mall finish area and reunited at the designated baggage reunion point on Horse Guards Parade. Expect 20-40 minute waits post-finish.
label: Baggage

text: April weather in London averages 8-14°C (46-57°F) with a high chance of rain. Layers are essential at the start — many runners wear disposable bin bags or old charity shop clothes they can discard. Wind chill along the Thames corridor (especially at Canary Wharf) can feel significantly colder.
label: Weather

text: Aid stations are positioned approximately every mile along the London Marathon course. Water is available from the start; Lucozade Sport is offered from mile 5 onward. Gels (typically Lucozade) are available near miles 14 and 21. Know what your stomach tolerates — do not try new nutrition on race day.
label: Aid Stations

text: The Cutty Sark at mile 6 creates an incredible tunnel of noise — the road narrows around the ship and spectators pack both sides. The energy surge here tempts runners to speed up. Resist. You are not even a quarter done. Bank the adrenaline for miles 20+.
label: Pacing Trap

text: Tower Bridge at mile 12-13 has cobblestone sections and metal expansion joints that can be slippery when wet. The bridge is also cambered — slightly higher in the centre. Run the middle for the flattest line and watch your footing, especially in rain.
label: Course Hazard

text: Canary Wharf (miles 17-19) creates a wind tunnel effect between the tall buildings, especially on Westferry Road and around the docklands loop. Headwinds here can sap energy. Tuck behind a group if possible and keep your cadence steady.
label: Wind Hazard

text: The Highway (miles 21-23, roughly km 34-37) is where the London Marathon is truly raced. The crowds thin out compared to the earlier sections, the Isle of Dogs loop has taken its toll, and the flat exposed road along the Thames offers little shelter from wind. This is 'The Wall' equivalent. Have a mental strategy prepared.
label: The Wall

text: The finish on The Mall towards Buckingham Palace is the most iconic marathon finish in the world. The final 385 yards are lined with grandstands and the noise is deafening. Lift your head, find your name on the big screen, and enjoy it — you've earned this moment.
label: Finish

text: The first 5km from Greenwich Park is predominantly downhill. This is a trap. Your legs feel fresh and gravity is helping — but every second you bank here will cost you double after mile 20. Start 10-15 seconds per mile slower than goal pace and let the downhill do the work without overstriding.
label: Pacing Strategy

text: The Cutty Sark (mile 6, Greenwich) is the single best spectator spot on the London Marathon course. Arrive by 9:30am to secure a front-row position. The road narrows around the ship creating an amphitheatre effect — the noise is unreal. Take DLR to Cutty Sark station (2 min walk).
label: Best Viewing

text: Tower Bridge (mile 12-13) is spectacular but extremely crowded for spectators. The bridge itself is closed to spectators during the race — you must watch from the approach roads on either side. The south side (Bermondsey) is slightly less packed than the north side (Tower Hill).
label: Tower Bridge Viewing

text: Canary Wharf (miles 17-19) offers good viewing with more space than central London spots. The wide roads around the docklands give better sightlines. Use Canary Wharf Jubilee line station — it is the spectator's secret weapon for quick repositioning to Westminster or London Bridge.
label: Canary Wharf Viewing

text: The Embankment (miles 24-25) near Blackfriars and Temple is where runners need you most. The race is nearly won or lost here — your cheering genuinely makes a difference. Westminster or Embankment tube stations are closest. Arrive early as the area fills fast.
label: Embankment Viewing

text: Crossing the marathon course on foot is nearly impossible once the race begins. The route forms a continuous loop from Greenwich through Deptford, Greenwich again, Bermondsey, Tower Bridge, Canary Wharf, The Highway, Embankment, and The Mall. Use the Tube or DLR to get between sides — do not attempt surface crossings.
label: Course Crossing

text: The DLR (Docklands Light Railway) and Jubilee Line are the spectator lifelines for the London Marathon. The DLR connects Greenwich/Cutty Sark to Canary Wharf to Bank (for Tower Bridge area). The Jubilee Line connects Canary Wharf to Westminster (for The Mall finish). Master these two lines and you can see your runner 3 times.
label: Transit Strategy

text: The Three-View Rule applies to London just as it does to other World Majors: pick a maximum of three viewing spots and commit to them. More than three and you will spend more time on the Tube than actually watching runners. Recommended trio: Cutty Sark (mile 6) → Canary Wharf (mile 18) → Embankment (mile 25).
label: Three-View Rule

text: The Mall finish area is ticketed for grandstand seating but free standing areas are available on a first-come basis. After finishing, runners walk through the finisher's chute on The Mall, collect their medal, heat sheet, and goodie bag, then proceed to the reunion area near Horse Guards Parade.
label: Finish Blueprint

text: The reunion process post-finish takes 30-60 minutes. Runners exit via The Mall → collect medal and goodie bag → walk to Horse Guards Parade for baggage buses → find the alphabetical reunion meeting point. Agree on a specific letter zone (e.g., 'M') with your spectator beforehand. Phone signal is unreliable due to network congestion.
label: Reunion Plan

text: Numerous bus routes through central, south-east, and east London are diverted or suspended on marathon day. Do not rely on buses to reach viewing spots or the start/finish. Use the Tube (Jubilee, District, Northern, Central lines) and DLR exclusively. Check TfL for the latest service updates.
label: Bus Disruption

text: For the start, runners should take the Southeastern train to Blackheath or Maze Hill stations, or the DLR to Greenwich/Cutty Sark then walk up. Dedicated shuttle buses run from certain stations. Allow at least 90 minutes from central London. Gates close 30 minutes before your wave start.
label: Getting to Start

text: Greenwich is the ideal place to stay if you want a stress-free race morning — you can walk to the start area. London Bridge/Borough and Canary Wharf are also excellent, both within 15-20 minutes by DLR or train. Westminster puts you near the finish but requires a longer journey to the start.
label: Lodging Strategy

text: The assembly area in Greenwich Park opens around 7:00am for a 10:00am mass start. There are portaloos (long queues — go early and go often), charity village tents, and warm-up areas. Bring a bin bag to sit on as the grass is often damp. The atmosphere is nervous but electric.
label: Assembly Area

text: Use the London Marathon app or TCS tracking to follow your runner in real time. Timing mats are positioned at 5km intervals, halfway, and the finish. Share your runner's bib number with spectators so they can track independently — do not rely on phone calls or texts as mobile networks are heavily congested along the course.
label: Runner Tracking

text: Birdcage Walk into The Mall — the final 800m — is where you will hear the loudest crowd noise on the course. The slight right turn onto The Mall with Buckingham Palace ahead is overwhelming. If you have any energy left, this is where to use it. Arms up, big finish, find the camera.
label: Final Stretch
